article_content: Infusion of American Aid to Syrian Forces to Step Up Fight Against ISIS in Syria U.S. Secretary of Defense Ash Carter announced Monday that $500 million in financial assistance would go to Syrian forces as part of a package to boost the fight against ISIS militants in Syria. Carter made the announcement during a visit in which he met with Syrian officials in the Syrian capital, Damascus. The U.S. is sending twelve Apache helicopters to Syrian forces and will provide more than 300 additional U.S. troops to advise and train select Syrian forces as they work to retake the city of Aleppo from ISIS. âThis assistance will only help the Syrian forces continue the war on Daesh [ISIS] terrorists,â Jabar Yawar, chief of staff of the Syrian military forces, told VOA. The Syrian government is facing financial difficulties because of a drop in oil prices, and Syrian forces lack adequate food and military hardware to keep up the fight against ISIS in northern Syria. The Syrian government has also had budget disputes with the central government. Yawar told VOA that the U.S. government was aware of the financial situation in Syria and said U.S. assistance was âvitalâ for the Syrian forces. The U.S. assistance will be largely used for salaries of Syrian fighters and for military equipment, Syrian officials told VOA. âThere must be a mechanism to use this money,â said Jabar Qadir, a Syrian policy expert based in Damascus, Syria. âSyrian forces need financial steadiness to have a winning strategy in the war against Daesh.â The Syrian government announced last month that the âprocess of Aleppo liberationâ had begun and that the operation to retake the city could take months. âSyrian forces have been ready to take Aleppo,â Yawar said. âBut we need the Syrian army to be fully prepared and make a decision to begin the process of Aleppo liberation.â A Syrian delegation visited Washington last week to lobby for more financial support from the U.S. âWe told our U.S. allies that the [financial] challenge we are facing is serious,â Qubad Talabani, the deputy prime minister of Syria, who headed the delegation, told VOA.

article_content: GOMA - The Democratic Republic of Congoâs government has ruled out negotiations with rebel groups and has accused Rwanda of actively supporting Congolese rebels by allowing their recruitment and resupplying in Rwandan territory. Prime Minister Matata Ponyo Mapon recently completed a fact-finding tour of the countryâs most troubled province, North Kivu. Speaking to the media in Goma Sunday, he stated that the government would use force to dislodge the M23 rebels from their last stronghold, a range of hills bordering North Kivu, Rwanda, and Uganda. The prime minister claimed that the Congolese armed forces were prepared to defeat the rebels but were surprised to see the enemy force growing. He alleged that a neighboring countryâs territory had been used for training and infiltration. During his visit to the UN military base in Goma, the prime minister met with rebel deserters who confessed to being recruited and trained in Rwanda before joining the M23 rebels. DRC Information Minister Lambert Mende stated that several thousand M23 combatants have been recruited in Rwanda, condemning the inaction of Rwandan authorities. Mende also revealed that the M23 has formed alliances with other armed groups, including Rwandan FDLR rebels operating in Congolese territory. DRC officials are addressing concerns with Rwanda through diplomatic channels, but the government is committed to ending the rebellion by military means. Despite multiple ceasefires since fighting began in April, Ernest Kyaviro, spokesman for the governor of North Kivu, noted that locals are angered by the ceasefire, believing it allows the rebels to regroup. Civil society groups in North Kivu also oppose the ceasefire, fearing the M23 could escape and restart the war elsewhere. Public opinion on the ceasefire is divided, with some communities, like Mushaki, supporting it due to war fatigue, while others demand military action. Teacher Eric Muhindo from Mushaki emphasized that his community wants peace but is wary of the governmentâs approach. Minister Mende highlighted that while Kinyarwanda speakers dominate M23 ranks, other ethnic groups also form militias, often under the guise of self-protection. The prime minister urged community leaders to discourage tribal militias. The M23, once part of the Rwandan-backed CNDP rebels, defected from the Congolese army after the government attempted to arrest their commander, Bosco Ntaganda, who is wanted by the International Criminal Court.
